sections.hypothesis: Holding each pair towards its higher-yielding currency, only where the interest-rate difference beats the broker's 1% financing markup, earns a positive Sharpe after spreads and financing, 2006-2022, before the forex holdout: the interest collected each night is not fully taken back by the high-yielders falling.
sections.rationale:
Who pays: the carry trade earns the rate difference that uncovered interest parity says the exchange rate should take back, and on average doesn't. The published explanation is a risk premium: high-yield currencies fall hardest in global crashes, when carry trades unwind together, so the investor is paid for holding crash risk (Lustig, Roussanov and Verdelhan 2011, 'Common Risk Factors in Currency Markets'; Brunnermeier, Nagel and Pedersen 2008, 'Carry Trades and Currency Crashes'; Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen and Vrugt 2018, 'Carry', which finds carry earns across asset classes). Some of the payers are central banks and hedgers who are not trying to earn it.

Why this note now, DISCLOSED: it was proposed the day forex trend failed (findings 25), after seeing that financing, chiefly the broker's markup on a leveraged book, took more than trend's edge. That finding is why the rule only holds a pair where the rate difference beats the markup: below it the position pays to be held. The rule and its settings come from the papers and the measured markup, not from any forex carry result; nothing about carry on this data has been looked at. The sizing (3% volatility per pair, 60 days, 3x cap) is copied unchanged from the trend note rather than chosen again.

Risks stated before running: carry is known for sudden crashes, and 2008 is inside the period (AUD, NZD and the yen crosses); from 2009 to about 2016 rates were near zero in most of these currencies, so few differences beat 1% and the book will often be small or flat. The 10 pairs share currencies: a yen-funded book is long AUDUSD, NZDUSD, USDJPY, EURJPY and GBPJPY at once, one bet several times. Not a rejected family. The second trial in the forex pool.
sections.rules:
Implementation fx:carry (kestrel.strategies.fx_carry), all 10 [fx] pairs, daily OANDA candles with weekend candles dropped. On the first trading day of each month (New York), for each pair: the base and quote currencies' OECD 3-month interbank rates as published by then (the month before last, kestrel.data.rates.known_rate); long the pair if the base rate exceeds the quote rate by more than 100 basis points, short if it is lower by more than 100, else flat; sized to 3% a year by the standard deviation of the last 60 daily log returns as of that day, times sqrt(260). The weights stand for the month. If the sum of |weights| would pass 3x, all are scaled down together. Trades fill at the next open through kestrel.backtest.fx_engine: bid and ask, the 2% no-trade band, financing each calendar night at the month's own rates less the 1.0% markup, profit and loss in AUD.

One run: kestrel fx-backtest --research <this note> --warmup-from 2005-01 --start 2006-02 --end 2022-12 --cash 500. Nothing from 2023 (the forex holdout) is touched.
sections.parameters: threshold_bps 100 (the 1.0% financing markup measured from OANDA: the smallest difference a position earns on), vol_days 60, target_vol_pct 3, max_gross_pct 300 (all three copied from the trend note). Rates: OECD 3-month interbank, monthly, as published by the decision (month before last). From the engine and config: 2% band, 1.0% markup, 500 AUD.
sections.costs: Spread from the data on every fill; financing every night on the notional at the month's own rate difference less the 1.0% markup. A carry position earns financing by design, but only the part of the difference above the markup, and only if rates don't move against it within the month. Monthly decisions keep turnover low. One run, the second trial in the forex pool; at most three if (6) is reached.
